overview.description: While 'Hoyle' is best known as an authority on rules, the name is specifically synonymous with 'English Whist' - the game Edmond Hoyle first standardized. English Whist is a classic trick-taking game for four players and the direct ancestor of modern Bridge. It emphasizes memory, partnership communication, and tactical trump management.

history.origins: Standardized by Edmond Hoyle in his 1742 treaties 'A Short Treatise on the Game of Whist'. Before Hoyle, whist was a folk game (Ruff and Honours).
timeline: 1742: Edmond Hoyle publishes the first set of formal rules.
18th-19th Century: Becomes the most prestigious card game in Europe and America.
1890s: Modern Bridge begins to displace Whist in social status.
Present: Remains the template for all partnership trick-taking games.
history.evolution: The game evolved from the simpler 'Ruff and Honours' by eliminating the 'ruffing' phase and focusing entirely on trick-taking with a revealed trump.
history.cultural: To 'play according to Hoyle' became a global idiom for following the rules precisely.

setup.dealing: All 52 cards are dealt face-down, except the final card which is turned up to determine the Trump suit.

rules.objective: Win tricks for your partnership. Points are scored for each trick taken in excess of 6 (the 'book').
rules.gameplay:
1. Player to the dealer's left leads the first trick.
2. Players must follow suit if possible.
3. The highest trump wins the trick; otherwise, the highest card of the suit led wins.
4. The winner of a trick leads the next.
keyRules: Follow the legal action constraints defined for Hoyle.
Round outcome is resolved by the scoring method: Each trick above 6 counts for 1 point.
Winning condition: Win tricks for your partnership.

strategy.basic: Always try to 'return your partner's lead'. If they led hearts, lead hearts back to them later to help them win their high cards.
strategy.intermediate: Third-hand high: The third player in a trick should generally play their highest possible card to secure the trick or force a higher card from the fourth player.
strategy.advanced: Card Counting: Keep track of every trump card played. Knowing when the opponents are 'out' of trumps allows you to safely dominate the table with your remaining long suits.
tips: Don't lead from a suit where you only have the King; you'll likely lose it to the Ace.
Leading a singleton (a suit where you only have one card) can be a good way to use your trumps early.

list.name: Honours
list.description: Partnership holding all four top trumps (A K Q J) scores 4 extra points; three of the four scores 2. Tricks are scored first; a side at 4 points cannot score honours on that deal. Many players omit honours to reduce luck.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Scoring variant only; no engine constant overrides.

list.name: Fixed trump sequence
list.description: Trumps cycle in order: hearts, diamonds, spades, clubs (and optionally no trumps every fifth hand). Used in whist drives and tournaments instead of turning the last card.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Trump determination method; no numeric overrides.

list.name: Game target and rubber
list.description: British: game is 5 points; rubber is best of three games (first to win two). American: game was often 7 points. Long Whist: game is 10 points. Tournaments often use a fixed number of deals and total odd tricks as score.
list.emptyOverridesReason: Scoring target varies by region; no single engine constant.
No fourth named variation documented in primary sources.

difficulty.medium: Basic 'third-hand high' logic; understands trump priority.
difficulty.hard: Expert card counting; partnership signaling simulation; probability-based defensive play.

considerations: Card counting (tracking trumps and high cards).
Leading heuristics (Returning partner's suit vs finding voids).

additional: Edmond Hoyle - A Short Treatise on the Game of Whist (1742)

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck with four suits and thirteen ranks per suit; no jokers. Games 'according to Hoyle' typically use this standard pack for whist, rummy, and other classic card games documented by Hoyle.
engine.suitDescription: The four French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) each contain thirteen cards. Suit determines following and trump in trick-taking games and is used for melds in rummy-style games.
engine.rankDescription: Standard ranks Ace through 2 in each suit; ranking (Ace high or low) depends on the specific game. Hoyle's rules apply to a wide range of games using this standard rank set.
